episode_title: Keep the Property Income and Lose the Management with Alan Fruitman, Ep. 817
question: What exactly is a triple net property and how does it differ from a regular commercial property?
transcript_excerpt: A triple net property means the tenant takes care of everything—all taxes, all insurance, all maintenance. If the roof leaks, if the roof needs to be replaced, roof structure, parking lot, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, everything means everything. As a landlord you can be on a boat in the middle of the ocean, never visit the property, play golf, travel the world, and not have to babysit your property.

episode_title: Keep the Property Income and Lose the Management with Alan Fruitman, Ep. 817
question: Why do major corporations like McDonald's and Chase Bank lease properties instead of buying them outright?
transcript_excerpt: McDonald's makes more money selling hamburgers than owning real estate. If they spend $3 million to own a building, they could instead open three new locations and leverage that $3 million into income from selling burgers at three stores. The banks loan money, restaurants sell food, Firestone puts on tires—they make more money from that than owning real estate. If they own the building, depreciation works one way, but if they pay rent, it's 100% deductible that year, which is a tax advantage.

episode_title: Keep the Property Income and Lose the Management with Alan Fruitman, Ep. 817
question: What are the two key ingredients Alan Fruitman identifies for long-term success in triple net property investing?
transcript_excerpt: You want to find great real estate—location is always number one. And then you want a great tenant, number two. So it's a dual guarantee. Your rent is guaranteed by the credit worthiness of that tenant. But if the worst case scenario happens, like Blockbuster Video, what do you have left? You have the great piece of real estate. So that's why location matters.

episode_title: Keep the Property Income and Lose the Management with Alan Fruitman, Ep. 817
question: How do you identify a great tenant versus a decent tenant in triple net property investing?
transcript_excerpt: You want to find an industry that AI, Amazon, and the Internet won't replace. When you're hungry and need an inexpensive hot meal, you go to Chipotle or McDonald's—it's a permanent need. Blockbuster Video got replaced, but Firestone Tire won't because you can't put on your own tires. You need somebody that can tell you the financial differences between McDonald's and Burger King and other competitors—they don't all have the same credit worthiness. McDonald's has stronger credit than smaller players, so you'd much prefer McDonald's as your tenant.

episode_title: Keep the Property Income and Lose the Management with Alan Fruitman, Ep. 817
question: What is the difference between a buyer broker and a seller broker in commercial real estate transactions?
transcript_excerpt: A buyer broker works for the buyer and doesn't care which property you buy as long as you get a great property—the broker gets paid the same amount on all properties, so there's no vested interest. A seller broker is code for representing the seller; their job is to sell you that one property. With a buyer broker, you get somebody on your team that educates you about the nuances and differences between properties, locations, and tenants, rather than trying to convince you to buy a specific property.
